utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue with the cross-examination of Witness Moroz, both parties have announced that there were some preliminary matters to be raised. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Just a few pieces of information. I have been asked to convey that General Mladic would ask to leave the courtroom after the first break and to return to the Detention Unit for personal reasons. We were not in a position to submit this in writing because there are technical problems in the Defence room. We cannot write that up because the entire system is down. The entire computer system is down. However, the general is prepared to confirm for the record verbally today that he waives his right to attend the session after the first break. Also, I wish to inform you, Your Honours, in view of you said yesterday the expert Dusan Pavlovic will testify in this courtroom next Monday. I believe that is the 14th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. I think we gave our decision on the expertise of Mr. Pavlovic yesterday. That's then clear. And that's Pavlovic, then -- that's in the context of scheduling for next week. That's well understood. Perhaps we could deal right away with the absence of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic, you have a right to be present. I do understand from Mr. Stojanovic that you waive that right for the next session. If you would please confirm that, then please switch on your microphone and confirm that you -- that it's your wish not to -- not to attend in the next session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have a family visit. So I would like to ask that, after this first session, I go back to the Detention Unit and let the lawyers continue their work, according to plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that extends for the rest of the day, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The entire day. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's your right to be present, Mr. Mladic. There's no obligation. Therefore, even without the approval, but the Chamber has to make clear that you waive the exercise of this right. That's then clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, Mr. Pavlovic is the first one to appear on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. He is the first witness on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And after Mr. Pavlovic, you have other witnesses for next week? As previously scheduled.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have another witness, Your Honour, the one that we discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's fine. That doesn't need any further explanation. Then we'll start with the examination of Mr. Pavlovic not yet. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, I didn't realise what you were indicating but if it is my opportunity to address the matters we wanted to raise in advance of the next witness, I'd like to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We can do that in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I wanted to address several matters. The first we wish to report back on a matter that the Court asked the parties to try to resolve and that was the question of armed conflict. The Prosecution and Defence have indeed, been discussing that issue with a view toward reaching agreement and we hope to report back shortly that we have indeed resolved this issue along with some related issues that have arisen during the discussion. That's not quite as concrete a report as we had hoped to make but I wanted to indicate that indeed steps were being taken in the right direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have an expectation that such agreement would be reached before Christmas or should we think in terms of 2016 if not 2017, Mr. Tieger? The Chamber has become wiser on the basis of its experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would imagine that my raising the expectation that we could resolve it before the recess would be probably the best way of ensuring that couldn't happen, but we will try to do. So we stay in contact and the issues don't seem to be so intractable that that's beyond the realm of realistic possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that Mr. Stojanovic is smiling so he must have the same expectations and we leave it open which Christmas it will be. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. At the same time, we've also maintained contact about the number of remaining witnesses and wanted to share that information with the Trial Chamber. In essence, there are three categories of witnesses left: The Tomasica experts; the 92 bis applications opposed by the Prosecution; and international witnesses. And all of these categories, as I'll indicate in a moment, are very limited. So, first, there are two Tomasica experts as the court is aware. Mr. Radovanovic, Mr. Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think Mrs. Radovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I'm sorry. There are two remaining 92 bis applications which are opposed, Matijevic and Miljanovic. And in the third category --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I have on my mind Simic and Miljanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Matijevic was opposed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And there are approximately six remaining witnesses in the third category of international witnesses. Because of the possibility that their appearances may implicate potential protective measures which we're not aware at the moment, I won't name them. We're advised that all of these witnesses involve some level of difficulty in obtaining their appearance, and accordingly, the Defence has indicated its intention to file subpoenas and for that reason the Prosecution anticipates that the Trial Chamber will wish to monitor progress on that front in much the same manner it has with respect to remaining experts. In any event, this difficulty, coupled with the likely completion dates for the expert reports, means that there is a high likelihood that the few remaining Defence witness will not be available to testify immediately after the recess, and, indeed, not in January. And this scheduling issue further implicates the Trial Chamber's earlier comments about final trial briefs and its expectation that the parties would be or had commenced work on those briefs and the Trial Chamber's reference to the possibility that, upon conclusion of the case, the parties might have a matter of weeks within which to submit the brief. Now, I imagine that you're already aware that we sought guidance informally on that timing and understand now that -- by that I mean that understanding is the understanding of both the Prosecution and the Defence. We share the information that was made available. That -- that was essentially a reference to the possibility that the formal end formal conclusion of the case might be protracted with considerable non-court time, during which considerable progress could be made on the brief. So by way of extreme example, if six months elapsed waiting for one final witness whose evidence involved one hour of court time, the time that the Trial Chamber would allot for the brief to be submitted, after consultation with the parties, would clearly be dramatically less than if the formal end of the case occurred today. And that's our understanding. But in light of that, and particularly in view of the likely January schedule, the parties appreciate that they need to be gauged in the final brief process. However, genuine progress on that front is dependent upon an understanding of how much room there is for discussion of any of the many issues involved. In other words, an understanding of the final trial brief word limit. Now, the parties have discussed that and agree that, in view of the scope and scale of the case, a word limit comparable to that allotted in the Karadzic case, 300.000 words is appropriate. And I had the opportunity to explain to Mr. Nilsson informally the multiple advantages to the parties and to the chamber that in our view that word limit provided. Accordingly, we hope that the Court is in a position to confirm that word limit if it sees fit, prior to the recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to understand. 300.000 words is approximately 700 pages, isn't it, if we have 400 words on a page, 40 lines, then words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, it depends on the number of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's more or less what we are thinking, in terms of anything between 500 and 800.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. President, I have captured with full accuracy the information that has arisen and exchanged during the course of our discussions with the Defence and appreciate the Chamber's time this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is there any response or any observation the Defence would like to make at this very moment on matters raised by Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just to confirm that intensive talks are underway on that topic with the Prosecution and, once again, I wish to inform you that we are seeking a solution and working as efficiently as possible on concluding the Defence case. We are in constant contact with our experts who are supposed to appear in court. So all new material that we receive will be forwarded to the Prosecution and to the Trial Chamber in good time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. I think the Chamber can add to this that decisions on 92 bis -- on pending 92 bis motions are -- can be expected, perhaps not all of them but at least some of them soon. Anything else in this respect? Looking at today's programme, I think the cross-examination of Mr. Moroz was scheduled for one hour and a half, and -- well, before the start, of course, there's no reason yet to say that you can stick to that, which means that most likely we'll finish somewhere in the second session today and have no further witnesses for this week and then we'll continue Monday morning with Mr. Pavlovic. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Only to mention, as the Trial Chamber is aware, that cross-examination will be conducted by Mr. File, and I will cede the floor to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Moroz.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that is, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. File. You find Mr. File to your right. Mr. File is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. File, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, in your testimony on Tuesday at transcript page 42349, lines 19 to 23, you said: "But there were several weeks when even on first floors water was absent and trucks with water tanks were organised to -- well, to bring water for the population and the main source of the water during that period was a big reservoir on the brewery, city brewery because it was the lowest point in the city." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter 33555, e-court page 8, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm going to show you your prior testimony in the Karadzic case which corresponds to transcript page 29544 to -45 in that case. Starting at line 14, you said: "Ah, so I meant people went down stairs to ground floor because there -- so the pressure of the water couldn't afford to go up to higher floors and took in tanks and in some -- anything where water can be put, they took water and went upstairs to their apartments. "Q. The difficulties that you were referring to, though, weren't just the inconvenience of going -- having to go downstairs and get some water, lug it back up the stairs -- "A. Mm-hm. "Q. -- was it? "A. Yeah. "Q. That was the only difficulty that you saw for the civilian population? " And on the next page of the transcript: "A. It was only one period, two or three days as far as I remember, that it was great shortage of water and trucks with water tanks were going around the old city and people took water out from these tanks." So my question is: When you said in the Karadzic case that this period lasted two or three days, should we understand that you were revising that testimony on Tuesday when you said that it lasted several weeks?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, well, I see that there is a contradiction in my words. As far as I remember, it was up to two weeks, the situation. Why -- let me continue one sentence more. I went to brewery and I know all the story, because I was asked by Ukrainian chief commander, battalion commander, to go to brewery and to agree with bosses there to bring water by tanks to Ukrainian battalion, and in Ukrainian battalion, the situation -- it is also very low, Tito barracks, the old city and very low, the lowest point of the town, and they brought by tanks -- by vehicles with special tanks, water tanks --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to battalion and it last three or four days. But for the rest of the people, it was up to two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. As we saw in the Karadzic case you also said that this was, "only one period." Did you mean to say that it was the only period during -- or between October 1993 and October 1994 when people did not have running water in their apartments in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that it was the only period. Probably -- but it was the only big enough, long enough period --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which people, all people kept spare water in their apartments just for the sake and they -- they can live more or less normally so they have enough stock of water for one to two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Can you remember when this period was during your time in Sarajevo, for example, which month it was?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in winter, definitely. No, I can't say for sure, but it seems to me it was in February, January or February.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: There were severe water shortages in Sarajevo from the moment you arrived in October 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Can we look at 65 ter 30669, please. When this comes up you'll see this is a weekly BH political assessment that's dated 26 October 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. File, the 65 ter number is given six digits. Can you say it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could look at page 3 towards the bottom, you see a paragraph that begins with: "WHO experts." It says: "WHO experts suggest that the biggest humanitarian problem facing Sarajevo at the moment may be water. Recent shelling has cut the electricity to the Bacevo pumping station and has further disrupted the water distribution system. In addition, the Serbs have now cut off water coming from Moscanica, the small backup system the city used to use when Bacevo was not functioning. The amount of available water in Sarajevo has consequently shrunk considerably. The incidents of Hepatitis A in the city is increasing. An epidemic is possible." Now does that accord with your recollection of the state of the water supply when you arrived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it's very -- it looks very much, describing the same period which I talked to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I would tender that document, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 30669 receives exhibit number P7774, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Do you remember an incident that occurred towards the end of your tenure in Sarajevo starting between the 14th and 15th of September 1994 when there was a storm that knocked out one of the main power lines serving central Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly speaking, I don't remember that story.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Can we look at 65 ter number 33551, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: When this comes up, you will see that this is an excerpt from an Agence France-Presse newspaper article from 15 September, 1994. In the middle of the page it says: "Sarajevo was deprived of water and electricity, Thursday, 15 September, after storms and separatist Serbs cut off supplies to the city. The cuts marked the first time the Bosnian capital had been deprived of power and water for 24 hours since a February cease-fire was agreed for the capital. "The UN Protection Force said one of the two main power lines into the city had been brought down by storms, while the Bosnian Serbs at Vogosca, north of Sarajevo, were diverting power from the second line to their self-styled capital, Pale. "The lack of power put out of action the Bacevo water-pumping station, which supplies Sarajevo with 80 per cent of its water." Were you aware that the Bosnian Serb side had the capability of diverting electricity supplies from Sarajevo to Pale?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure for 100 per cent but I suppose they have such possibilities because of this plant I have seen there were different lines in different directions and, of course, they can switch electricity on and off any of those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If there was an electricity cut to Sarajevo, then the water-pumps would stop functioning; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- the problem is that water field from where water was pumping on the tank, the biggest tank on the mountain of Mojmilo where -- on Serbian side, and that is why cutting off Sarajevo itself from electricity doesn't -- yeah, was not connected with operations on -- on these -- on those water fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. I understand your point about the reservoir. I'm just asking you about the water-pumps themselves. For example, at the Bacevo pumping station, if the electricity is cut to those pumps they will not function; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. And this gets to your point which is if the water-pumps stopped functioning then the only major source of potable water that would remain in the city --

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: -- is whatever was left at that moment in the Mojmilo reservoir or any underground pipes?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question. Do you have knowledge about all these pumping systems et cetera, for example, are you aware of any urgency facilities to have electricity produced locally? Do you know something about it or is it just that you assume, as it is usually everywhere, that water is pumped up in a reservoir that from the pressure from the reservoir, it comes down. Do you have any specific knowledge about the systems and especially the solutions in case of electricity cut.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not a specialist in water supply. I'm a military and I had several missions of renovations damaged some parties of the water supply system of Sarajevo, there was a big problem with engines which were pumping water from the area I told you in Ilidza, I don't remember the specific -- Ilidza is a big area close to Sarajevo, and there were probably a dozen of engines which should pump water to the highest point above Sarajevo to tank and then from this tank, water was going down to Sarajevo and was used by population, industry, so on and so forth. I renovated -- organised renovation of probably ten of engines on this field, and after renovation, I also was on the highest point on the -- Mojmilo, and I have seen maps with -- how tubes all these pipes are going down to the -- Sarajevo. And I -- I -- I saw myself how water is pumping or not pumping, how closed wells and open wells and what -- the results were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any specific knowledge about generators for electricity --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've not seen them, but you also do not know what they --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've seen, because I also renovated -- organised, organised renovation by specialists, some pylons, some parts of power plant because UNPROFOR supplied in significant amounts special oil for -- for pump -- for electricity industry where this -- for this power plant, for instance, and I delivered, in tanks, this oil to Serbian workers, and I must control that this oil is filled in special system to start the operation of the plant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- yes, I see that for general electricity plants. Were there any provisions for emergency electricity generators for the water system or don't you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a follow-up. Sir, when you say you organised the renovations and you organised the repairs, what you actually mean? And the question I really want to find out is: Were you actually part of the team of technicians who did the job? Or were you just somebody who tried to find technicians from wherever you could find them and they did the job, and while they did the job, you saw the pipes as you say you saw them and you saw how things looked like. Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So my job was, after receiving order to go somewhere and renovate something, either electricity line or water supply system, whatsoever, I contacted specialists on -- one -- one of the warring sides, sometimes both of them, and informed them that we are ready to organise that mission for renovation of this or that facility object. After receiving their reply, positive reply, that they're interested in that, I informed that our liaison officers who should agree that mission with warring sides military -- with military representatives. And then with a convoy, military -- small military unit, I should gather all workers, engineers involved in the mission to deliver them to the point of our job to -- to ensure their security, and after our -- after end of the job, to get them back to -- to the sites where I took them from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So you were not part of the technicians. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Getting back to this question of the water-pumps, when they would stop functioning, were you aware that that would lead to a drop in water pressure and water could not be supplied to apartments and houses?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And do you agree that the Bacevo pumping station supplied Sarajevo with about 80 per cent of its drinking water?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say what the percentage of that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it surely was the greater part, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour I would tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33551 receives exhibit number P7775, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And just to be clear, this Bacevo pumping station was in Bosnian Serb-held territory in Ilidza; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember that at the same time that the electricity and water supplies were cut off in mid-September 1994, Bosnian Serb authorities also turned off the natural gas supply by closing the gas valves they controlled in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me it is a surprise, because I was absolutely sure that no gas supply took place during my whole tour of duty because when speaking to civilians inside Sarajevo, they never told me that gas appeared. Because I -- I thought it was cut in the beginning of hostilities and --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And -- they never had gas supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So your recollection is that there was no gas supply to Sarajevo during the entire time you were there --

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter 18780, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: When this comes up, you'll see that it's a weekly report of the office of the special co-ordinator for Sarajevo for the week of 12 to 18 September, 1994. It's dated 19 September 1994, sent to Kofi Annan and Yasushi Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can we get the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, we're back began on the B/C/S. Could we have English to the right of our screens. Yes, there it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You'll see from the beginning of this document, it says: "The week under review was dominated by the most lengthy and comprehensive shut down of utilities which Sarajevo has experienced since the dark days of last winter. A combination of storm and war damage completely cut the electricity supply on 14 September. With no electricity to operate the pumps, this inevitably led to the water supply into the city coming to a halt. On 15 September, the" -- and for the B/C/S we go to the next page. "... the gas supply was cut. Information obtained by technical experts of this Office, UNPROFOR engineering units and other sources suggest that the gas supply was almost certainly interrupted by Bosnian Serbs closing valves in the part of the city which they control." Were you part of the UNPROFOR engineering units described here that determined the gas supply was almost certainly interrupted by the Bosnian Serb side closing valves that it controlled?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not remember that any of the officers of the unit I was part of was involved in gas problem of that period. I told you that in the beginning of my tour in Autumn 1993, only twice I visited gas stations, one visit on Bosnian side, and one visit on Serbian side, and no gas problems appeared in the conversations and tasks of our unit. Probably it was some other unit of UNPROFOR or ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly requested to move to the microphone so that he speaks into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So the visit that you were discussing on Tuesday when you met with the director of the Bosnian Muslim gas company and the Bosnian Serb gas company, that took place in Autumn 1993?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at the next paragraph of this document. It says: "In spite of extensive efforts being made I UNPROFOR at all appropriate levels, the week ended with gas still turned off and without the necessary clearances having been obtained to enable work to begin on repairing the electricity lines. A meeting at the technical level, at which this Office was represented, took place at the airport on 18 September. This meeting revealed that there was comparatively little disagreement between the parties on the technical problems involved, but the necessary repair work to restore the electricity and gas supplies still awaited clearance at the political level." So when this document says, "the necessary work still awaited clearance at the political level," do you understand that specifically to mean that the technical people could fix the power lines but the Bosnian Serb leadership was not letting them have access to the places where repairs had to be made?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection. Misstates the document and the evidence. Nowhere does it say Bosnian Serb leadership. We don't know which political level is being discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't say anything on that question because I was not involved in the meeting which you have referred to, and -- so level of my competence was lower than the question you are asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. And next time if there is an objection, if you could just wait for there to be a ruling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's one. Second, of course, Mr. Ivetic, Mr. File referred to the document saying political level and then ask a question about that level, which was leading by the way. He did not misstate the evidence and there was no reason to intervene. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender that document please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do so, the political level could also include the Muslim side, couldn't it? The two sides might have had to agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That may be the case and that's why I was seeking the witness's view on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 18780 receives exhibit number P7776, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter number 33552, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: When this comes up, you'll see it's a "New York Times" article published 25 September 1994. Starting with the first paragraph, it says: "Sarajevo was sealed tight today. Threats to aircraft from the Bosnian Serbs closed the airport. All roads out were barred. Deprived of water, as well as electricity and gas for ten days, people holding plastic containers formed long lines at the Miljacka river. "It was the 904th day of the siege of Sarajevo. The sun shone, gun-fire was intermittent, people pushed wheelbarrows full of water containers slowly up the hills." Now, people had to go down to the Miljacka river to retrieve fresh water because it was one of the points where the water-pipes were at the lowest elevation in the city; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me if this article is correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm asking about the water-pipes near the Miljacka river, if those were at the lowest elevation in the city.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. I'm not sure, but -- this area, indeed, is very low concerning other parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you saw people in -- waiting in long lines for fresh water; correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, my person opinion that magazine articles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, we are not seeking your opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question. You said you did not see people waiting in long lines for fresh water. You said that was not -- you -- would you like to add anything to that answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from opinion. If you want to say what you did see perhaps, then -- or wait for the next question by Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay I will add what I saw. September, I'm surprised that a lot of things now appear that September was a period of hostilities. September, August, September and October was the period when people felt everybody knew that peace is coming. No shooting inside Sarajevo at all. It was the period when UNPROFOR people got permission to walk around the city freely. And personally me, with several officers, start jogging along the Sniper Strasse, the most dangerous area during hostilities. And now I see that some hostilities, some water shortage in September, I don't remember any water shortages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, you said no shooting inside Sarajevo at all. No shells fell on the city, no incidents of shooting, for example, sniper incidents occurred.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. Inside Sarajevo, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We got permission not to wear flak jackets and to walk freely around the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In that case, I'd like to clarify something that you said in your Karadzic testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could look back at 65 ter 33555 at page 9, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Starting at line 4, you were asked: "Q. It's the case, though, isn't it, that civilians lived in constant fear when they had to venture outside their homes to get food and water? "A. Of course civilians suffered from the situation when each day there was a risk that water can be cut -- could be cut. "Q. But the water was cut on a number of occasions and the civilians had to risk their lives lining up to get water, did they not? "A. So of course it took times and efforts to take water. "Q. And sometimes they were queueing up for days in order to get water? "A. I can't say for this, no, no. Probably one day, yes; two days, I hardly say -- even the two days they couldn't get water. And -- because the next day these tanks with water started driving around the old city and people queuing -- of course queue -- they waited in queues just to get possibility to fill their tanks with water." Now in your previous answer it is suggested that you didn't see people standing in lines for water. In your Karadzic testimony, it sounded like you did see. Can you provide an explanation as to what you saw in terms of people standing in line for water.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- in both cases, we discuss different periods of my staying in Sarajevo. I just told you that in September 1994, I saw no queues and no use for queueing for water, because no hostilities were. And more or less all systems started functioning more or less normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: But what you just read, we speak about winter of -- winter, January/February of 1994. It was earlier than September 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter 33554, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you'll see, when this comes up, it's a "New York Times" article from the 26th of September, 1994. It says: "The Bosnian Serbs reopened the gas supply to Sarajevo today after a 11-day cut-off but they ensured that the airport remained closed by threatening to shoot at incoming United Nations flights. "The airport, which runs between Bosnian Serb and Bosnian government positions, is essential to the arrival of food aid to the city and to the United Nations peacekeeping operation. A spokesman for the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, said current food supplies were sufficient for another two weeks. "The agreement to reopen a critical gas valve closed by the Serbs in the suburb of Ilidza west of the city was reached at a meeting of senior Bosnian Serb and Bosnian government officials. An outline accord was also reached on repairing sabotaged electricity pylons, but no electricity was expected to reach Sarajevo for at least two more days. "Because electricity is needed to pump water into homes, the 300.000 people of Sarajevo remained without running water for the 11th consecutive day. "The main traffic in the city now consists of people pushing wheelbarrows, shopping carts, baby carriages and other makeshift contraptions loaded with water taken from pipes near the Miljacka river." Do you recall during your time in Sarajevo observing people pushing these wheeled devices loaded with water taken from pipes around the city?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. It was the winter of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So this description here, would you say that this is an accurate description of what you saw in the winter-time but not in February?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: But no summer of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When you say -- may I ask you this: Winter of 1994, do you mean winter 1993 to 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Or winter 1994 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The most difficult -- it seems to me, as far as I remember, the most difficult period for common people inside Sarajevo was January and February 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. File, may I ask you clarification. You said so the description here, would you say that this is an accurate description of what you saw in the winter-time but not in February? For me in a northern hemisphere, February is still winter.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I agree that it is and I intended to say September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I take it that you understood the question as such, Mr. Moroz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That you said you didn't see it in September?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm absolutely sure that in September, no such picture could be seen inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I jogged around the city, and I saw a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... you did not see this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender that document and I believe it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I was actually going to object to this one. If the document doesn't reflect what the witness saw, I don't know if it is appropriate to introduce a newspaper article that has not been confirmed by the witness as being accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness did confirm the accuracy of the document. He just applied it to a different time-period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you mean he testified about the description, a description which is found in the document. Do you withdraw the objection or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Stand by the objection. This is dated September. So the document proceeds to apply this to September, which the witness said that is not the case so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. It is relevant even if the witness contradicts parts of what is described. That's not a reason for non-admission. Please proceed -- no, no, we do not proceed. We first hear from Madam Registrar the number assigned to this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33554 receives exhibit number P7777, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And just to clarify, Your Honour, I believe it needs to be MFI'd pending a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there's no translation - I didn't check that - then the status is not admitted but marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not always a B/C/S translation was required and sometimes documents have been admitted even when there was no B/C/S translation, but you raised the matter yourself. There was no objection. Do you stand by that you'd rather have it admitted with a B/C/S translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In that event, it may not be necessary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No major problem, Mr. Ivetic. Then I again change now the status from marked for identification to admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because earlier today you tendered a document also without a translation, P7775, Mr. File. So that -- and there was no objection to that either. We take a break but we'll take the break slightly longer. The Chamber might wish to -- to consider among ourselves to see whether we are already in a position to give any guidance on the matters raised by the parties earlier. Therefore, we take a break slightly longer. Mr. Mladic will return to the UNDU, I take it, for that transportation, everything has been prepared. The witness may follow the usher, and we'd like to see him back in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we resume, a few practical matters. First of all, and I'm addressing you, Mr. Stojanovic, do you confirm that the Defence is not in a position to bring a substantial number of witnesses in the month of January or that the difficulties are such that we'd have to fear that most of the time would not be filled?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. For the reasons that are well known to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This having been confirmed, the Chamber has considered these problems and has decided that we would re-start after the winter recess on Monday, the 1st of February. Therefore, no sitting in the month of January. We know that for the Tomasica experts, it's still rather unclear when we would hear their evidence, but then the Chamber expects you to be fully prepared for calling the six international witnesses and, to the extent needed, also any witness for which 92 bis applications will be denied, if there are any such witnesses. So that should then follow without further gaps in February. This also means that the Defence, because we have heard about all the problems and possibly need -- that there is a need for subpoenas to be issued, but no motion for a subpoena has reached the Chamber until now for those witnesses, and, therefore, without delay, you should work on that so that the Chamber can provide the assistance you need to do what we expect you to do; that is, to examine those witness in the month of February, without gaps in time. Finally, about the word counts, whether it should be 300.000, 200.000, or 400.000, the Chamber will consider that. The Chamber will also make a comparison. The Chamber will think about it, and before the winter recess we'll hear from us what number of words are allowed in the final briefs. We leave it to that, although there are a few other matters, but we leave them to this Monday. Any questions about this? Any -- if not, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. The Chamber suggests that we would -- in one session hear the evidence of the witness in cross-examination and in re-examination. We are not limited to the one hour which we usually apply if Mr. Mladic is present. So, therefore, it's our aim to conclude today's session in the -- this very same session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With the witness. And I may have a few court agenda items, but these are very short ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, Mr. File will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please look at P6555.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: When this comes up, you will see that this is an UN document from one day after the newspaper article we were just looking at, it is briefing by special representative Akashi to Kofi Annan, dated 27 September 1994. Under utilities, part a, you see: "The gas supply is back to normal, based on agreement between Karadzic and Izetbegovic to open gas valves." Under b, it says: "Electricity (see attachment) repairs have begun on the Sarajevo network following Karadzic's agreement to clear the access of repair team, provided UNPROFOR subsequently also addressed the problem of the eastern and northern Bosnia power lines of particular interest to the Serb civilian populations: "1 repair at Kokoja completed which now provides power to Ilidza (6 megawatts), Blazuj and water-pumping station at Bacevo (4 megawatts). "Vogosca pylon being repaired as we write and, therefore, electricity supply should soon be restored to central and eastern Sarajevo: "3 Kiseljak line, east of Raljevo to be repaired tomorrow thus providing electricity to Buca Potok, Western Sarajevo." If we could go to page 2. That doesn't seem to be the correct page 2 in the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This seems to be the correct page. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It is the correct page.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If you look at point c, it says: "Water --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then we should move to the next page in B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: It says: "Water, as a result of b(i) above, Bacevo station is functioning again and water is beginning to reach western Sarajevo (including PTT building)." So now earlier you saw an UN document describing when utilities were cut. Now you see an UN document describing when things were brought back on line. So my question is: Isn't it possible that you have forgotten about this episode in September 1994?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the problem is that during Autumn/winter after my arrival in Sarajevo there were weeks with problems described like that, and in summer and in September, all the problems appeared but they diminished to hours, maximum days and that is why people, me including them, didn't pay much attention to it because our life was already organised to the way that we get used without water in taps because we had some stocks. People used to live with shortages of electricity so -- and it was a warm period.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that --

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: -- this type of incident where the utilities are cut for 11 days you might not remember that specifically?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, because I'm absolutely sure that probably there were some periods of switching on both water and electricity for short periods for -- for people just to -- to make stock.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because so long period, 11 days without water and electricity, I am absolutely sure it would be -- I would remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Let's look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question in this context. You also earlier told us there was never any gas as far as you remember during the whole period. Now we see in late September that it is before you left that the gas supply is back to normal. So apparently -- do you allow for the point that you may have either missed some information or that you may have forgotten some elements of what happened at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once I told you here probably the first day of, that what I know about life of people inside Sarajevo, it's from their words and of what I've seen. And in winter, when people suffered a lot, they -- they complained to me that no gas, no warm -- hard to survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and they didn't speak to me -- in summer they didn't speak about gas and I didn't ask them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If they don't speak about it, for you, it seems that there is no gas or that there is gas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see it is a gap in my information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- for that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's understood. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could please look at 65 ter 33441.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This is a document from the water supply and sewage disposal systems public utility company, the JKP, Vodovod i Kanalizacija which covers the period from April 1992 to October 1995. If we could please go to page 6 in the English and the B/C/S, this is from the introduction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which period does it cover, Mr. File?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: April 1992 to October 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In the first full paragraph at the top of the page, it describes that this report was drafted by a working group of the Sarajevo water utility in late 1995. And in the third full paragraph, in the middle of the page, it says that it was based on duty books and documentation possessed by the company's general manager and section managers. If we could go to page 65 in the English and page 84 in the B/C/S, which is in the section covering 1994, four paragraphs down, under September you see from 14 to 27 September (1100 hours) there was not a single well in operation due to an electricity shortage. "On 27 September (1100 hours), and until the end of the month, there were only two wells in working order, which is 18 per cent of the capacity (one for the direction of Mojmilo reservoir and one for the direction of Alipasin most), out of the 11 in working order." So if the Bacevo pump was functioning at 18 per cent capacity, this would also result in very low water pressure and supply to the reservoir; correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. The last document I want to show you regarding this utilities incident is from the same day; it's P6714. This is a letter from the City Assembly of the Serbian City of Sarajevo addressed to RS President Karadzic, the president of the National Assembly of RS, and the president of the government of RS from the 27th of September, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could go to English, the bottom of page 4; also page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: At paragraph 9, what you see is: "In the most recent using of Sarajevo for the purpose of raising and lowering tensions in the whole of former Bosnia and Herzegovina (the cutting-off of electricity, water, and gas) about 40.000 households in Serbian Sarajevo have suffered considerable financial damage. The damage is estimated at around 10 million German marks. "The Assembly believes that such activities should be carried out with prior consulting and informing of the political organs of the municipalities and city and finding the mechanisms to evenly distribute the financial damage thus created among other regions in the republic as well." Now, this reflects how the utilities network in Sarajevo was set up in such a way that if you cut off the electricity, the water, and the gas to Bosnian-held Sarajevo, you were necessarily also going to deny these services and bring harm to at least some Serb-held civilian neighbourhoods as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Now, based on the information that we have looked at, you would accept that Bosnian Serb authorities shut off the water, the power and the gas to Sarajevo for at least 11 days in September 1994; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't deny or support that because we don't know the real reasons of that. Probably some technical things because my section was not involved in the repair during this case --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that is why I am not -- I know nothing about this political and all this information exchange and I -- I told you that it was not due to hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I would like to go a different period in your time in Sarajevo, February 1994. I'm going ask you about Scheduled Incident G8, which is the shelling of the Markale market-place on the 5th of February, 1994. On Tuesday, you were talking about your observations of the crater --

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: -- I just wanted to clear up an ambiguity in the transcript at T42370, lines 8 to 9. The Presiding Judge asked you: "Do you have any special training in interpreting?" And then your answer was: "No, no." Just to make sure our record is clear, I will ask you do you have any special training in interpreting traces or craters from mortar explosions?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Do you have any special training or expertise in ballistics?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not special. Only in both cases, the first question and the second, only general, like military general imagination of what is going on in this or that case, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And the same is true for explosives as well?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you didn't see any official investigation reports at the time?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: On Tuesday, at page 42365, you talked about the height of the buildings. And you said the trajectory of the shell couldn't be so close to the building. But you didn't know what the trajectory of the shell was; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we look at P538, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps one question in between. Did you ever measure any of that, that is, the height of the building and the distance between the building and the place where the shell landed? If there was a shell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- but people, civilians knew in that very place where can work and where they do not work never because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you have explained that in your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This is an excerpt from the UNPROFOR investigation report for that incident. You were shown this document by my colleague Ms. Sutherland when you testified in the Karadzic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could go to English page 3 and B/C/S page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we could have an English version on our screen as well. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: During that Karadzic testimony, you were also shown this page containing the signature of Lieutenant-Colonel N. Rumyantsev at the bottom right corner of this page; correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And during that testimony your attention was drawn to paragraphs 12 and 13 towards the top of this page under findings which confirmed the conclusions that the explosion was caused by a conventional 120 millimetre mortar and had been fired in a convention manner and detonated upon impact with the ground; correct? You recall being shown that?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And those conclusions are contrary to the conclusions that you say that you heard from Mr. Rumyantsev; correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: In the Galic case that was transcript page 18173, which is page 51 of D1370, you said you didn't know if he signed anything at all because you hadn't seen the report and you said that you saw no reason why he would tell you things contrary to the findings of the team's report. And in your Karadzic testimony, after seeing this report, you were asked whether this was still your position and you confirmed that it was. That was page T29543. Is that still your position today?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Immediately after Markale I, there was a cease-fire; correct?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: After this incident, after this explosion in the market-place, there was a cease-fire; hostilities declined?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And that was effective in terms of reducing the shelling and the sniping that had been going on in Sarajevo up to that point; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And the combat at that point was low in intensity; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Became less intensive, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Can we look at 65 ter 30744, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This is going to be a document from 9th of February, 1994 so four days after that shelling incident. It's an UNPROFOR status report.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could go to English page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Under electricity, the second half of that comment says: "During several high level meetings between Silajdzic and Krajisnik in January, it was agreed to repair the line Raljevo-Buca Potok, which is essential for the distribution of electricity to the people of Sarajevo. Still, clearance for this repair mission has not been given by Pale yet." Now, do you recall participating in any repair missions of that electricity line in the immediate aftermath of this cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am -- I was during that period, I was involved in several repair mission on pylons, destroyed pylons, but I don't know if -- it were the part of that line or some other lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I -- I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: With a reduction in hostilities that would have been a good time to do those repairs?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, each time when the hostilities, the intensity became lower, our missions of renovations of civilian facilities intensified.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I would tender that document, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 30744 receives exhibit number P7778, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we please look at 1D00058.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This is going to be a document from roughly two weeks after the shelling in the market-place. It's another weekly BH political assessment; 17 February 1994. It will be page 2 of the B/C/S and 1 of the English. The second point you see, it says: "Sarajevo is calm. The present cease-fire is by far the most effective ever made -- despite major differences between the parties as to what they are expected to do." If we go to page 3 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S, please, five paragraphs down, you see: "The humanitarian situation in Sarajevo is relatively good. Water, electricity and gas are still very limited, but food has been flowing in well. The lack of adequate supplies of especially gas is particularly important as Sarajevo is in the grip of the coldest weather this winter: Night-time temperatures have been falling to below minus 20... centigrade. The Bosnian government claims that the valves on gas supply lines have been turned off by the Serbs, who deny this and said that the problem was originated in Serbia." Were you aware of how civilians managed to stay warm during winter-time without adequate supply of gas for heating?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They used wood and sometimes they created some handmade ovens just to burn wood in them and thus.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to show you a document from about one month after the cease-fire. This is 65 ter 33009. This is another weekly BH political assessment from 9 March 1994. Here it says: "Peace appears to be breaking out in much of Bosnian." And it notes that Sarajevo remains mostly calm and there is a growing sense that war will not return to the city. And if we could go to page 2 in both versions, please. About two thirds of the way down it says: "Despite these developments there are number of obvious obstacles to full normalisation. "The city is still entirely dependant on humanitarian aid for food. There is very little water, fuel or electricity. And the main roads in and out of the city remain blocked by the Serbs." Does this accord with your recollection that the city was calmer than before the cease-fire but there was still very little water, fuel or electricity?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, during ceasefire the situation is calmer. For sure. But all this facility -- facilities which supplied some things inside Sarajevo were damaged a lot, and they needed -- in several places, and they needed some time to be renovated.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender those two documents we've just looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 1D00058 receives exhibit number P7779. 65 ter number 33009 receives exhibit number P7780, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could look again at number 33441, which is the water utility document we looked at before.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm going to take you through what happened with the Bacevo pumping station during this relatively calm period.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could go to page 56 in the English and page 72 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Under February, and this is the 1994 section, it says: "During this month, the city's biggest water supply problems were caused by power failures at the Bacevo source, and these occurred on 8, 9, 11, 20, 21, 25 and 26 February." If we could go to the next page, please, in English. About four paragraphs down, it says: "Since there was a lot of work to do at the Bacevo source," and then it describes the work that needed to be done. It goes on to say: "Our teams of qualified workers were set to go there but they had already been waiting 20 days for UNPROFOR to give them clearance. Doing the above-mentioned work would much improve the relation redness of the Bacevo source and, consequently, water supply to the city." Now, for UNPROFOR to give clearance for a team of Bosnian workers from Sarajevo to go to the Bacevo pumping station to do repairs, that would have required receiving permission from the Bosnian Serb authorities; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. Both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could go to March which is -- in English, it's same page at the bottom and B/C/S, it's page 72. It says: "Our facilities mostly had a regular supply of power. However, the amount of water" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, English where?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: At the very bottom of the page under March, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: "However, the amount of water supplied to the city was modest because our teams of qualified workers did not manage to go to the source to do the necessary repairs of the wells and equipment in order to supply quantities of water." If we could go to the next page in English and B/C/S, please. About four paragraphs down, it says: "The situation at the Bacevo source was worrying because of the extent of the breakdown of the wells and the equipment. UNPROFOR, however, could not enable our teams to go to the source and eliminate the breakdowns." Now, I take it you do not specifically recall escorting a team of Bosnian workers to make repairs at Bacevo during that month?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We started renovation of that equipment a little bit later.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at April, which is the next page in English and it's page 75 in the B/C/S; next page as well. Here it says: "During the month, we had problems with power supply to the Bacevo source and facilities in the city, which adversely affected the operation of the wells and, consequently, water supply to the city." And then it describes how seven wells at Bacevo were usually operating and nine were out of order, meaning it was operating at 44 per cent of its capacity. Then it says: "Our teams of qualified workers were unable to go to Bacevo to make the necessary repairs of the wells and equipment." Now if we could go to May, which is English page 60, B/C/S page 77. At the bottom of the page, it says: "With the help of UNPROFOR, teams of our qualified workers managed to go to Bacevo and so a number of wells were brought into operation, which resulted in increased water supply to the city." Next page in the English, please, and also next page in the B/C/S. Four paragraphs down, it says: "On the 25th our teams of qualified workers were allowed access to the source, with UNPROFOR escort. Consequently, two wells (B3 and B4) supplying the Alipasin most pump station were brought into operation, so that the source was operational at 63 per cent of its capacity, or ten wells ..." Do you recall whether you participated in this repair mission to Bacevo in the 25th of May 1994?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't support now the exact date of the mission, but I should say that it -- it were a number of missions. It took around two, probably three weeks, not everyday activity but probably each other day, activity of that repair works.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because just let me explain why. Because, first of all, we were -- there was a reconnaissance, reccy mission like we called it, because people, specialists, went there to find out what spare parts needed, and they start gathering some parts from one engine, one well, to install -- to ignite broken engines. Then from ten, for instance, make operational two or three. And then they order some spare parts through UNPROFOR logistics, some logistics departments --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And this process started in May of 1994?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask you about something you said on Tuesday at transcript page 42349. You said: "There were difficulties with the water supplying because there were periods especially during winter when pumping stations in Ilidza, where water was pumping into the mountain of Mojmilo were not operational due to -- sometimes the reason was lack of electricity and for some period, it was around two months only, there were around 11 dozen -- sorry, there were around a dozen of engines pumping water and only several of them were in operation and that was there was a -- it was a lack of water in reservoir in Mojmilo." So this episode that we were just looked at, where Bacevo was operating below its capacity, is this the episode that you were referring to in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And you would acknowledge, after seeing this documentation, that although you said it was around two months, in fact, it was over three months?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you around two months, because time has passed and I recollect just my general idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. And the key problem here was getting access to make repairs; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this Chamber has also heard evidence that only four days before the team of Bosnian repair workers was given clearance to go to Bacevo the VRS Main Staff issued an order transmitting Radovan Karadzic's instructions not to obstruct the flow of water, electricity or gas without his permission. That's P6557. And when you were in Sarajevo, were aware of any such instructions from the Bosnian Serb political or military leadership?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, a month or so later, from June into July 1994 Bosnian Serb forces were shooting at or near the UNPROFOR repair teams again; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: During summer, this period was very calm. And I do not remember to be shot at during my mission at that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we look at P6553, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do that. I remember that you might have mentioned this on Tuesday but I just wanted to reconfirm: How were the qualified working teams constituted in terms of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were -- we have chosen not in accordance with the ethnicity but in accordance with their professional knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. But did you take -- I thought you mentioned something like taking some people from the Bosnian side of the war and others from the Serb side of the war, irrespective of ethnicity but people coming from opposing camps. Is that what you understood you to say last time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were various cases. For instance, as far as electricity line reparation, pylon reparation, there were specialists only on Serbian side. As for sewage system clearance, only on Muslim side. Sometimes I told you that, for reasons I already mentioned, there were joint teams when they -- they wanted to be sure that everything was done correctly, spare parts installed, so on and so forth. But as far as water field renovation, specialists were only on Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could look at -- I see it's come up now, P6553. This is a meeting -- minutes of a meeting at Sarajevo airport on electricity. The top of the first page you see several UN representatives present, Lieutenant-Colonel Ricquet of UN BH command and Major Cirefice listed as number 5. Did you know either of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If we could go to e-court page 2 for both versions, please. Under paragraph 2.1, you see it says: "Major Cirefice reported that repairs are being performed on two lines, Velesici-Kosevo and Vogosca-Kakanj. He said that much time had been lost on the line Velesici-Kosevo because of shooting from both sides. Works on the line Vogosca-Kakanj had been stopped because of shooting from Serbian side close to Ilijas." If you look down at paragraph 2.4, it says: "Lieutenant-Colonel talked about problems between BSA and UNPROFOR. He said that Serbian side obstructs the works by shooting at the teams. Are the works going to be performed or should the teams be withdrawn? The repairs on electric power networks are also political problem. These repairs are being performed on BH side but not on BS side." So does this refresh your recollection as to the amount of shooting that was takes place during this period in 1994?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I missed what date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This is the 7th of July, 1994.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollections say that shooting, sniper shooting, diminished by that period significantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
