utterances.text: And they were just -- so, you see, my -- my estimation were that they were just joking. I was several -- personally, me was several times shot at, but each time traces of bullets were just close to my legs. I am absolutely sure that if they wanted to kill me, they would kill me because they were good snipers, good specialists.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If they were wanting to interfere with repair missions, they were succeeding; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: On Tuesday you also talks about occasions where your section chief said that certain water valves or wells were found closed off or turned off in Bosnian Muslim-held Sarajevo, that was T42350. Now, it's true if you have a weak water flow or a weak water supply, closing some wells or valves could increase the water pressure to neighbourhoods where the valves were left open; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And if you alternated the valves that were open in different neighbourhoods, you could distribute water across a greater part of the city over time; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the system was rather complicated. I can't neither support or disprove you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Did you receive any briefings when you arrived in Sarajevo in October 1993?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And did you ever learn, either through a formal briefing or through informal conversations, that before you arrived Sarajevo Ratko Mladic had used the possibility of restoring the water supply that had been cut off from Sarajevo as a negotiating tool with your colleagues at UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't heard anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter number 08230, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. File, are you testing the recollection of the witness or are you seeking to establish that that's what happened? Because if that -- the latter is the case, why would you do that through this witness who said that he didn't hear about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Well, this shows -- it is the latter, Your Honour, and it shows the extent of the witness's knowledge, what he was aware of as well as how he may have interpreted certain events that he saw while he was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's also testing the recollection of the witness that what he would have known or should have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's the first and the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: That's a better way of putting it, yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This is 23 July 1993 report from UNPROFOR headquarters to -- in Sarajevo to UNPROFOR HQ in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: If you look at page 1, paragraph 1d, it says: "To ensure his co-operation, Mladic gave details of road and bridge repairs that he wished to see made. Moreover, he asked for the water supply to be reinstated by UNPROFOR in the town of Donji Vakuf. This was given as a prerequisite for the restoration of water to" -- And if we go to the next page: "... Sarajevo." So this was something that did you not hear, either through a briefing or any conversations with your colleagues at UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because the day I arrived, the same day they went home after they finish of duty, so I didn't have chance to communicate with guys who did the job I did after them.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I would tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if the witness doesn't know about it, he has tested the recollection of witness with the document and it hasn't caused witness to change his testimony then I'm a bit concerned that we're trying to introduce a document through a witness who doesn't know anything about the document, and that is exactly the former of the two options that Your Honour made rather than the first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would expect the witness to know about this information, and the fact that information exists is the other half of the equation, so I think it would assist the Trial Chamber to have this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. File, that would justify introducing whatever information that exists just on the basis of that you expect for whatever reason - and you may have some reasons for that - that the witness would be aware of it. I think you read the relevant portion of the document which apparently was knowledge available at the time. The admission is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I just have a couple of questions about your answers on Tuesday regarding hearing from a Russian peacekeeper that he saw Muslim soldiers crossing the river at night-time. Do you recall giving that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: You were quoted from your prior testimony at transcript page 42360 as having said: "The officers [sic] told me that soldiers went from the old city, crossed the river, and then went in a south direction up to the hill, where -- which was the area of Serbian forces -- the position of Serbian forces. Well, and during the day the fire was done in the direction of the old city." First of all, just to clarify: You never saw this yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And were you aware that the confrontation lines went through the Jewish cemetery and all the way up the hill to Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember just names of that area, but it was the hill just along so-called sniper strasse.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Could we look at P3, page 76, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Here you can see the confrontation lines marked in blue and red, with blue representing the Bosnian Serb side and red representing Bosnian Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: This shows the area to the south of the river with the elevation of Debelo Brdo roughly in the middle. Does this refresh your recollection of the names of those features and the positions of the warring parties at that time?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Novo Sarajevo, yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And were you aware that the Muslim side had its own positions on this hill?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally me --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment. Because I -- I just look at the map. Well, I never seen Muslim positions in that area. I don't know -- no trenches -- I don't know what they used for -- for that, but in that area, I haven't seen positions of Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. Last set of questions. You spent -- on a few occasions today, you talked about the difficult times during the winter between --

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: -- 1993 and 1994. If we could have 65 ter 33008, please. This is an UNPROFOR fax from Akashi to Andreev regarding security of civil affairs staff in BH dated 18 January 1994, and it encloses a 13 January memorandum from Cedric Thornberry, the head of civil affairs, to Mr. Akashi. If we could go to English and B/C/S page 2, please. You'll see that paragraph 2 of this memo states: "All civilian officers working in Sarajevo have been in life-threatening situations during the last few weeks, near-victims of sniper attacks and mortar bombs. They are constantly having to decide between not doing their jobs effectively and risking their lives." If we can go to English and B/C/S page 3, please. Under paragraph 4, it says: "For UN peacekeeping, all staff participants accept a level of risk which would otherwise be intolerable. But the BH situation has been getting worse in recent months - not only in Sarajevo. Sarajevo and Mostar now rank with Kabul and Mogadishu as amongst the most dangerous places in the world." It goes on to say: "Accommodation is often insecure and movement to and from places of work and residence is habitually hazardous in Sarajevo." Now, during this period, 1994, January and before, you were fired on while attempting to carry out your duties in repairing utilities lines; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: And was some of that fire from the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say who -- who fired at me. It -- at my mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. You were also fired on while travelling between your accommodation in the Marsal Tito barracks and your headquarters in the PTT building; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I would tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33008 receives exhibit number P7781, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. One question for you, Witness. If you say, I can't say who fired at me, do you mean to say that you couldn't even tell us whether you were fired from both sides when you did your missions or that it was ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The problem of identification of the source of shooting was that the greater part of that was from the area -- neutral zone area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I also realised I may have omitted to tender number 33441 before, which was the water utility document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's 84 pages, isn't it? You want us to read all of them, where you used three or four?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to read all of them, although it is a resource that covered the entire period of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. File, if you present it into evidence, all of it, we read all it. And, therefore, just to say, We dealt with those, the whole of the document, the usual solution for that is that you make an excerpt of relevant pages and that you -- perhaps with a cover page, if need be, and perhaps specifically in relation to the pages mentioned also the in-between cover pages where it says, This is 1994 so that we have a clear orientation as far as timing is concerned. Before we decide, Mr. Ivetic, do you have any objections against --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have an objection to the whole thing coming in when we've not had evidence or witnesses to authenticate the document and to discuss what's in it. So, yes, I have an objection to the whole thing coming in. I don't have an objection to what Your Honour has suggested, which is the selection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Could we then hear from you, Mr. File, what is the origin of the document. And, Mr. Ivetic, if you have any specific concerns about the -- about the authenticity of the document, please convey to us what they are. But, first, for you, Mr. File.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The pages from the introduction that I referred to at the -- during the first use of that document describe the -- its provenance and what it's based on, which is a working group from that public utility company, and that the information is based on their own records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you There. I mean, if I write a document saying that I, the president of state X, issue a certain order, then saying the authenticity is proved by just saying, Well, that's what the document says. Of course, authenticity is a problem, and I was primarily interested in provenance, where did you find it, was it in an archive, rather than to say, That's what the document says. Because there's no dispute about that, I take it, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Our records show that we've received it from AID Sarajevo on 5th of April, 2000. That's the information that we have in our evidence records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And does it say anything about where AID got it from? Because I don't know whether the AID is usually keeping the records of water supply companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: I don't believe that information is indicated, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Would you please try to find out whether there is any other knowledge about it. And now I'm addressing you, Mr. Ivetic. What are your specific concerns about ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I appreciate that you supported my idea that we should have an excerpt rather than whole of the document, but I think you still had concerns remaining, authenticity. Could you specify what especially supports your suspicions about the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Throughout this trial, we've had numerous objections as to questionable documents that have come from AID which, again, is the secret police in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We've had the witness -- testimony of a witness from that service who talked about the head of the AID basically talking about how to fix a trial and talking about illegal activities that were undertaken by that agency. That was Mr. Garaplija. So under those circumstances, and as Your Honours rightly pointed out, it is kind of strange that documents supporting -- purporting to be from a utility company are in the hands of the secret police of that same entity. It would be different if they got it from the Serb side; but if it's purported to be from the government side and it's coming through the secret police, I'm a little bit -- I don't see how it would get into their possession. They're not - to my knowledge - the custodians of such records. The utility companies themselves would be and the Ministry of Energy would be. So to say a document came from the secret police raises great suspicions in my mind. Again, I don't know, because we've just received this document for the first time in the notification for this witness so I have not had a chance to do any investigations on the Defence side. I'm just always hesitant to see a large document of 84 pages that we're told comes from the secret police and might talk about all sorts of things, since I haven't read it all, to have the whole thing come into evidence without having a proper witness to talk about these things and to see whether what's in that document is actually always 100 per cent accurate or reflects confirmed information. That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There's nothing in the document itself - I mean, inconsistency in information or something of the kind - but your suspicion is that it may have been an 84-pages falsification of a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Or that parts of it are. I don't know. We've just received it. I haven't had a chance to read all 84 pages, to be quite honest, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just add if you look at the parts of the document that we've examined today it is corroborated by other UN documents, by newspaper articles, the descriptions of the time-periods for shortages are corroborated within both this document as well as -- as other submissions that we've made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I appreciate what you've said, but does that argument you are putting go to saying you don't want a page of this document admitted, or are you prepared to accept excerpts?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I've said already once and, Your Honour, Judge Orie has said it. I don't have a problem with the excerpts that have been confirmed by this witness to come in. That's not a problem. The problem is the whole 84 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So an excerpt would not -- despite your doubts as to authenticity, would, nevertheless -- would not for those pages where the witness testified about events. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. File -- yes, then I may have misunderstood you in that respect, and Judge Moloto apparently was listening better to you. Mr. File, if you -- you know that no admissibility issues arise if you upload the relevant pages you dealt with. I leave it in your hands at this moment whether or not to persist or to choose that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- that's -- that's fine. We're happy to tender excerpts. I would also include the introduction which describes the nature of the document which we looked at briefly for clarification. And just for the record, we don't believe that this is a fabrication in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you'll show to Mr. Ivetic the excerpts before you finally upload them and see whether there's any disagreement about what portions. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I also do understand it is very limited, the initial pages and, apart from that, timing and the pages you used.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll ask Madam Registrar to already reserve a number for those excerpts still to be uploaded.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P7782, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That number is reserved. Could we hear from you after you've discussed the matter with Mr. Ivetic. And I know the winter recess is coming close, well, let's say, before Christmas, and it doesn't make any difference anymore now which Christmas it is because we'll not be sitting in January. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So final document I want to show you is 65 ter 33553. I just want to show you a description of life in Sarajevo roughly six to seven months after the February cease-fire during the utilities cut-off that we were discussing at the beginning of this cross-examination. This is from the 19th of September, 1994. I'm going to read the first five paragraphs of this and then ask you a question. It says: "Six months after a NATO ultimatum stopped the Serbian shelling of Sarajevo, this city has entered a nightmare-ish twilight zone in which the horrors are less palpable than exploding shrapnel but more insidious and just as destructive. "Deprived of their freedom surrounded by green hills that mock them with their inaccessibility, often without water and electricity, people complain of living in an agonising limbo where the adrenaline caused by terror has been replaced by mounting anxiety and a wave of depression. "'The feeling now is of being in a room with all the windows closed,' said Jasmin Spahovic, a policeman. 'When I think of the coming winter, I think of having to burn my furniture for heat. We're broke, we're surrounded, and we feel like animals in a zoo.'

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: "Doctors, psychologists and social workers say stress-related illnesses in Sarajevo have soared to unprecedented levels over the past few months. Dr. Zeljko Trgrancic, a psychologist at the Kosevo Hospital, said one-quarter of hospital beds were now occupied by people suffering from what he called post-traumatic stress disorder. 'In the first phase of the war, there was shock, but people still had reserves of strength ... but this year, since the shelling eased off, we have seen mounting suicide, depression, apathy, and alcoholism. We estimate that stress disorders in the city are now at nine times pre-war levels.'" So my question for you is: Even in light of your observations of the civilian activity that came after the February 1994 cease-fire, you don't exclude that this description of the civilian population in Sarajevo in September could be accurate; right?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to my mind, he -- this article -- so shifted a little bit accents to the worst side. Because my personal experience in relations with journalists, I made several interview. I gave several interview to journalists from -- rather respected journalists, and when I read with my photo the article which arrived after my interview, I read nothing what I told a journalist about.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Okay. When --

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is why I should say there is -- I accept that people suffered a lot and stress was very big. And when the situation became calmer, all the stresses came around and they suffered a lot. It's psychological. But as far as the whole atmosphere of the city is concerned, I see nothing of the kind that I have seen because it was -- September was a period of hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: So to clarify, when you were speaking of the civilian population trying to get on with their lives and regain a sense of normalcy during the cease-fire, you would still accept that, under the surface, they may have been deeply scarred by the traumas?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. Surely. Surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. File. Mr. Ivetic, any further questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do. Just shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you started telling us about your own personal experiences dealing with interviews given to the media that were not, I guess, accurately recorded. What about the situation that you saw in Sarajevo? How was the media reporting about what was going on in Sarajevo? How did it compare to what you were seeing during your tour? Do any other -- apart from your interviews, do any other incidents come up in your memory that did not accord with what you were seeing in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, inside PTT building officers discussed a lot. The reflection in media, the situation in Sarajevo. And the general -- the general impression was that no -- how to say it? No relevant information were reflected in media. No -- neither in Russian, neither in Ukrainian, what we have access to. No Americans, no British, no French. I don't read French, and I ask French officers what French journalists TV says about the situation in -- in -- and they answered me: Lie like everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you the following in that context. Now and then we've seen media reports -- and I'm not taking any position as to the accuracy, but sometimes this Chamber was able to verify the accuracy on the basis of other documentation, whether that would be reports, UN reports, BiH reports, Bosnian Serb reports, whatever. Are you saying that whatever was written is always wrong anyhow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I'm speaking about media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm talking about media as well. You say whatever they write in the media, it's -- it's not true anyhow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All media stands on lie or other side. And it is -- sometimes lie is 1 per cent, really, when I read magazines in Sarajevo, I am asking myself, Where I am now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say it's -- it wasn't -- it's often not objective. If you say lie was 1 per cent or did you want to say that lie was 100 per cent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's my personal estimation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if lie is 1 per cent then there's still 99 per cent truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But sometimes 1 per cent is more important than 99 truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. I leave it to that. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you to clarify your previous answer. You said that you don't read French and you asked the French officers what the French journalists and TV say about the situation. And what is in the transcript I'm not sure records what you said that they told you. So could you again repeat for us what the French told you about the French TV and news.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that a lot of lie there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I think we have the full answer. One other item I'd like to talk with you about. It's a document that was used with you and it is now received the number P7779. And I'd like to have page 4 in the B/C/S, page 3 in the English, and if my notes are correct, it should be the fifth paragraph from the top. It's actually going to be the sixth paragraph from the top on the English. So this is just after the part that was read to you by the Prosecution where they stopped. And it says: "BH authorities in Sarajevo appear to be diverting even more food than usual away from intended beneficiaries. The civilian population of Sarajevo may be receiving less than a third of the aid brought into the city. It is not entirely clear what is happening to the balance: Some resurfaces on the black market; and some of it is diverted to the military; most, however, cannot be accounted for." Is that a situation that was discussed or known of within UNPROFOR in Sarajevo, that the BH Muslim authorities were diverting food from its citizens?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was commonly accepted. We even discussed that because we knew it for sure. Because we have seen in the market, products, some goods which were delivered by UNHCR, like humanitarian aid. And it was rather expensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I have no further questions for you. I'd like to thank you for your time and patience these last few days. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. File, any need for further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, this concludes, then, your testimony because the Judges have no further questions for you either. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, a long way to The Hague, for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, following the usher or leading the usher to the doorway is two different ways of moving in this courtroom. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're on your feet. I have a few court agenda items, but I'll give you first an opportunity to raise whatever you would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was in the public gallery this morning while Mr. Tieger was explaining our conversations, although he mentioned Defence, and he was talking to me, and since I heard that you might decide on the issue of the final brief on Monday, I was called by Mr. Ivetic since he was not privy with my conversation with Mr. Tieger to say and confirm or try to explain - not to deny - my conversations with Mr. Tieger. And although it was said at page 7, line 6, that Mr. Tieger thinks that he captured with full accuracy the information that has arisen and exchanged during the discussion with the Defence, at this moment, I have to differ, with all due respect, and I will try to explain our position. Maybe there was no -- enough understanding in between the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- bring to our attention whatever you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I want to emphasise to the Court that the Defence did agree with the OTP on the word limit, being 300.000 words, as Mr. Tieger stated. We also talked about the time needed for the final brief. The Defence position is that we would need nine months, and the Prosecution position is that they would ask for six months. The bottom line is that the Defence cannot start with writing the final brief before we file our bar table motion, and it's due on the 18th of January next year, as I remember. Every member of our team is involved in that task when not engaged with our witnesses. Also, we have to finish our work with the remaining witnesses, in particular, with our expert witnesses who require thorough preparation. We cannot commit ourselves to anything else before at least their testimony is complete. As there are only three of us, we do not have luxury that the Prosecution does to have numerous people to -- asking -- to assign tasks to. We believe that the time we have requested is a realistic and extremely reasonable given the circumstances. We can think maybe of six months only after our expert witnesses finish their testimony. That's actually the position of the Defence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for giving me the opportunity to clarify this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will consider the matter, and I said there are a few matters -- we briefly discussed during the break the submissions made by the parties, and we explicitly considered that the timing further down the road is not a matter on which we would decide now. There were too many uncertain elements in it, and the Chamber heard that Mr. Tieger was very much emphasizing that, depending on the time up to the moment where the case is closed, the Defence case is closed, that that would be a relevant aspect of the matter as well. But we have not yet, at this moment, considered it. But your position now is clear. And Mr. McCloskey is on his feet. And I think Judge Fluegge may have a question as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, before Mr. McCloskey responds. Just for my understanding, you said: "We can think maybe of six months only after our expert witnesses finish their testimony."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's where we mentioned also six months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Six months --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the finishing of the testimony of our expert witnesses, meaning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Until the deadline for the final brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you're again on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't want to complicate this, but please do not take as what Mr. Lukic said as the Prosecution requesting for six months. We have not made any specific request, and should the Court ask us to, we will. But I think we can take what Mr. Tieger said and leave it at there for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I mentioned what he apparently was emphasizing very much, that the time when we would not be sitting on a daily basis, perhaps waiting for a last portion of evidence, whether that would be experts or one witness who was not easy to reach or to get to The Hague, that that should be taken into consideration. That's what I understood what Mr. Tieger's emphasis was. Any other matter? If not, I have, as I said before, a few short court agenda items. I'll deal with them briefly before we adjourn. They are all remaining issues from the testimony of witness Mitar Kovac. First deals with Mitar Kovac's expert report, Rule 65 ter number 1D5358. In its oral decision of the 16th of July, 2015, granting Mitar Kovac the status of a military expert, the Chamber observed that some of the information contained in his expert report which is Rule 65 ter number 1D5358 is beyond the scope of the witness's expertise. The Chamber therefore advised the parties to focus their examination of the witness on those aspects of the report which relate to the witness's area of expertise, and this can be found at transcript pages 37478 to -481. Also, on the 19th of November during the witness's testimony, the Chamber noted on the record that there are some problems with the English translation of the report, and this is to be found at transcript page 41636. And in light of the foregoing, the Chamber requests the Defence to verify and correct the translation and to identify which portions of the report it intends on tendering into evidence. Next issue is about P7681. On the 19th of November, 2015, Exhibit P7681, a military report, was admitted into evidence. On the 23rd of November, the Chamber noted on the record a discrepancy -- that a discrepancy existed between the original document and the English translation and asked the Prosecution to verify and correct the translation. This is to be found at transcript pages 41701 to -702. On the 24th of November, the Prosecution informed the Chamber and the Defence, via e-mail, that a revised translation has been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 0205-6890-1-ET. And the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the old English translation of the document with the new one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if there's any issue with the new -- with the new translation or the -- then we'd like to hear from the Defence, well, let's say, not later than Tuesday. The last one is about "The Islamic Declaration." On the 18th of November, 2015, during the testimony of Mitar Kovac, the Chamber instructed the parties to agree which extract of "The Islamic Declaration" would be tendered into evidence; to be found at transcript page 41522 to -525. The declaration was previously marked not admitted without prejudice as D557. On the 19th of November, the Defence informed the Chamber and the Prosecution, via e-mail, that the proposed excerpt was uploaded into e-court under Rule 65 ter number 1D00172a. Any objection against this excerpt by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're going to need to just take a good look at that and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that. We often have followed the practice that we already instruct Madam Registrar to -- to -- to replace the old version -- oh, to assign the number and that we admit it but that you can revisit the matter within, let's say, before Christmas again. Because it is a bit more work perhaps. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to assign D557 to this excerpt as uploaded of which I just gave the number and admits D557 into evidence. And the Prosecution has an opportunity to revisit the matter before Christmas. Then we have one remaining issue from the testimonies of Zorica Subotic and Mile Poparic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The item I wished to address will not be addressed because some additional information on the matter contained in it was received by the Chamber. Therefore, we'll first look at that in more detail. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume Monday, the 14th of December, 2015, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th day of December, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.
